Btrfs stores checksums for each data block.  Until now
been stored in the subvolume trees
column2: indexed by the inode that is

column1: referencing the data block.  This means that when we read the inode
we've probably read in at least some checksums as well.
But
* The checksums are indexed by logical offset in the file.  When
compression is on
column2: this means we have to do the expensive checksumming

column1: on the uncompressed data.  It would be faster if we could checksum
the compressed data instead.
* If we implement encryption
column2: we'll be checksumming the plain text and

column1: storing that on disk.  This is significantly less secure.
* For either compression or encryption
column2: we have to get the plain text

column1: back before we can verify the checksum as correct.  This makes the raid
layer balancing and extent moving much more expensive.
* It makes the front end caching code more complex
the subvolume and inodes as we cache extents.
* There is potentitally one copy of the checksum in each subvolume
referencing an extent.
The solution used here is to store the extent checksums in a dedicated
tree.  This allows us to index the checksums by phyiscal extent
start and length.  It means:
* The checksum is against the data stored on disk
or encryption is done.
* The checksum is stored in a central location
following back references
This makes compression significantly faster by reducing the amount of
data that needs to be checksummed.  It will also allow much faster
raid management code in general.
The checksums are indexed by a key with a fixed objectid (a magic value
in ctree.h) and offset set to the starting byte of the extent.  This
allows us to copy the checksum items into the fsync log tree directly (or
any other tree)
column2: without having to invent a second format for them.
